title: Florida ADA Title II PDF Accessibility: 36 Cities Measured | SignalFeed.dev
description: How Florida cities of 50,000+ stand on PDF accessibility before the April 26, 2027 ADA Title II date: 27% of 1,662 sampled PDFs untagged, 10% scanned. Aggregate, automated signals.
h1: Florida: Title II PDF backlog in cities of 50,000+
body:
Florida has 56 cities of 50,000 or more residents with an official website listed in Wikidata. Under the ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35, subpart H), cities of 50,000 or more must make web content, PDFs included, conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA by April 26, 2027; smaller Florida cities and special districts have until April 26, 2028.

Does ADA Title II apply to Florida?

Yes. Title II is federal law and covers Florida's state agencies, counties, cities, towns, school districts and special districts; the PDF guide covers the rule's exceptions. This is general information, not legal advice.

We measured the PDFs these cities link from their public websites. This page summarizes Florida as a whole. It does not name or rank individual cities.

Florida at a glance

  • 36 of 56 cities measured with a usable sample (20 or more PDFs); together they are home to about 4.5 million residents. Of the rest, 8 blocked our crawler and 12 could not be sampled: too few PDFs on the main site (some host documents on other systems) or a crawl that only partly finished. That is not a clean result.
  • 1,662 PDFs analyzed. 27.5% had no accessibility tags, lower than the national figure of 40.0%. 10.3% were scanned images with no usable text, 32.7% did not declare a document language, and 41% had no document title.
  • Spread: in 6 of the 36 measured cities more than half the sampled PDFs were untagged; in 8, fewer than 1 in 10 were. The most common main issue was no declared document language (11 of 36 cities).
  • By size: in measured cities of 100,000 or more, 29% of sampled PDFs were untagged; in cities of 50,000 to 100,000, 26%.
  • 0 of 108 sampled PDFs passed the veraPDF PDF/UA-1 checks.
  • The median measured city has roughly 654 pages of PDFs failing at least one basic check; across the measured cities that is on the order of 70,000 pages.
  • 57% of the sampled PDFs were modified in 2024 or later. Recent documents are more likely to still be in active use, and documents used to apply for, access or participate in a service are not covered by the rule's exception for preexisting documents.

What this means for a Florida city

An untagged PDF gives a screen reader no headings, reading order or table structure, and a scanned one gives it nothing; both typically fail WCAG 2.1 AA. Archived content and preexisting documents are exempt unless people use them to get a service, so the usual order is: fix export settings, remediate forms and service documents, then move true archives to a marked archive section.

For agendas, minutes and notices, our accessible meeting templates for small public bodies ($24, Word + PDF/UA) export tagged PDFs from Word, so new documents start out accessible.

What this is, and what it isn't

These are automated signals scaled from samples, not a conformance evaluation: a check can show a PDF fails, not that it conforms. Method: national Backlog Index page.
